# Edited Nearest Neighbor {#sec-imbalanced-enn}

::: {style="visibility: hidden; height: 0px;"}
## Edited Nearest Neighbor
:::

This method is another undersampling method,
it works by removing observations close to the decision boundary between classes [@wilson1972enn].
This method tries to remove observations that would otherwise be hard to classify.

The algorithm goes as follows:

1. Compute the k nearest neighbors for each observation in the data set.
2. Remove observations from the majority class if the removal criteria are satisfied.

The removal criteria is something we can choose different options for.
A typical implementation will either remove an observation if the majority of the neighbors are of a different class,
but you could also tighten this and remove an observation if any of the neighbors are of a different class.

@fig-imbalanced-enn works through the majority-vote criterion one point at a time.

```{r}
#| label: fig-imbalanced-enn
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| fig-cap: |
#|   Edited Nearest Neighbor removes the observations whose neighborhood
#|   disagrees with them, which thins out the overlap between the classes.
#| fig-alt: |
#|   Four scatter plots in a 2x2 grid showing a gray majority class and a
#|   smaller pink minority class overlapping along a diagonal boundary.
#|   Panel 1: one majority point sitting inside the minority region has a
#|   dashed circle around it enclosing its five nearest neighbors, most of
#|   which are pink. Panel 2: because the neighborhood votes against it, that
#|   point is marked with a dark cross. Panel 3: the same test has been applied
#|   to every majority observation, and a handful of crosses appears on the
#|   majority side of the boundary. Panel 4: the flagged points are gone and
#|   the gap between the two classes has widened.
source("imbalanced-diagrams.R")

imb_data <- imb_toy()
k <- 5

neighbors <- imb_all_neighbors(imb_data, k = k)
disagreement <- imb_disagreement(imb_data, k = k)

# The majority-vote criterion, applied to the majority class only: a point
# goes if most of its neighbors disagree with it.
flagged <- which(disagreement > 0.5 & imb_data$class == "majority")

# A majority point that has landed inside the minority region.
focus <- flagged[1]
focus_point <- imb_data[focus, ]
focus_neighbors <- neighbors[[focus]]

e1 <- imb_base(imb_data, "1. Look at a point's k nearest neighbors") +
  geom_path(
    data = imb_ring(focus_point, imb_radius(imb_data, focus, focus_neighbors)),
    aes(x, y), inherit.aes = FALSE, color = imb_removed,
    linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_point(data = imb_data[focus_neighbors, ], size = 3.5, shape = 1,
             stroke = 0.7, color = imb_removed, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(data = focus_point, size = 4, shape = 16, show.legend = FALSE)

e2 <- imb_base(imb_data, "2. Most of them disagree, so the point goes") +
  geom_path(
    data = imb_ring(focus_point, imb_radius(imb_data, focus, focus_neighbors)),
    aes(x, y), inherit.aes = FALSE, color = imb_removed,
    linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_point(data = focus_point, aes(x, y), inherit.aes = FALSE,
             shape = 4, size = 3.5, stroke = 1, color = imb_removed)

e3 <- imb_base(imb_data, "3. Ask the same of every observation") +
  geom_point(data = imb_data[flagged, ], aes(x, y), inherit.aes = FALSE,
             shape = 4, size = 2.5, stroke = 0.8, color = imb_removed)

e4 <- imb_base(imb_data[-flagged, ], "4. The overlap has been cleaned out")

(e1 + e2) / (e3 + e4) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The idea is that we are able to remove noisy observations this way.
And depending on which criteria you choose, you could see how that would be.
By only allowing us to keep all the observations that have neighbors all of the same class,
we can end up removing a lot of the decision boundary,
especially any area where there is overlap.

The general framework is described in terms of 2 classes,
but it extends to more without any reduction, and so is one of the methods in @sec-imbalanced-multiclass that needs no expanding.
Both removal criteria are phrased as comparisons against the observation's own label:
the "any" criterion asks whether any neighbor carries a different label,
and the majority-vote criterion compares the observation's label against the most common label among its neighbors.
Neither question needs the other classes pooled together, and both look at the true labels throughout.

It does still change how things play out.
In the two-class case,
any majority point deeply embedded in the minority class will most likely be removed.
With three or more classes,
a single observation from one majority class deeply embedded in another majority class
will not only be deleted itself,
but will take its neighbors with it if we use the "any" criterion.
This feels less ideal and is something we have to think about when applying this method.

By itself, this method is simple,
and there have been a couple of method that expands on the foundation of this method.
The first one is **Repeated Edited Nearest Neighbor** [@tomek1976enn].
And it does what it says,
it repeats Edited Nearest Neighbor a number of times.
You can either set it up such that it runs a fixed number of times
or until no observations are removed during an iteration.

Another named variant **AllKNN**.
This is a variant of Edited Nearest Neighbors,
where you select a value of `k`, then apply ENN with neighbors `1` through `k`.
Both of these variants result in more observations being removed.

The last extension we will talk about is the **Neighborhood Cleaning Rule** [@laurikkala2001ncl].
This method starts by running Edited Nearest Neighbor.
Then we run a K Nearest Neighbors on the minority observations.
Any majority class observations that misclassify a minority observation will be removed as well.
Note that this second stage does not inherit the multi-class behavior of the first:
it needs to designate one class as "the minority", and the usual choice is the single smallest class,
with the remaining classes acting as a pooled majority.
That makes this half of the method the single-application strategy from @sec-imbalanced-multiclass rather than a true one-vs-rest.
Implementations typically also skip cleaning around classes that are themselves small relative to the smallest one.
@fig-imbalanced-ncl shows the second pass, which is where the two methods part ways.

```{r}
#| label: fig-imbalanced-ncl
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| fig-cap: |
#|   The Neighborhood Cleaning Rule adds a second pass to Edited Nearest
#|   Neighbor, removing the majority observations that get a minority
#|   observation misclassified.
#| fig-alt: |
#|   Four scatter plots in a 2x2 grid. Panel 1: the data after Edited Nearest
#|   Neighbor has already run, with a gray majority class and a pink minority
#|   class. Panel 2: one minority point whose neighborhood is mostly gray is
#|   circled, with lines drawn to its five nearest neighbors. Panel 3: the
#|   majority neighbors responsible for misclassifying it are marked with dark
#|   crosses. Panel 4: those points have been removed as well, leaving a wider
#|   margin around the minority class than the first pass produced on its own.
after_enn <- imb_data[-flagged, ]
rownames(after_enn) <- NULL

enn_minority <- which(after_enn$class == "minority")
enn_neighbors <- imb_all_neighbors(after_enn, k = k)

# Minority observations that their own neighborhood would get wrong.
misclassified <- enn_minority[vapply(
  enn_minority,
  function(i) mean(after_enn$class[enn_neighbors[[i]]] == "minority") < 0.5,
  logical(1)
)]

# The majority neighbors responsible are the ones that go.
culprits <- unique(unlist(lapply(
  misclassified,
  function(i) {
    nb <- enn_neighbors[[i]]
    nb[after_enn$class[nb] == "majority"]
  }
)))

ncl_focus <- misclassified[1]
ncl_focus_point <- after_enn[ncl_focus, ]
ncl_focus_neighbors <- enn_neighbors[[ncl_focus]]

n1 <- imb_base(after_enn, "1. Start from the Edited Nearest Neighbor result")

n2 <- imb_base(after_enn, "2. Find minority points their neighbors get wrong") +
  geom_segment(
    data = data.frame(
      x = ncl_focus_point$x, y = ncl_focus_point$y,
      xend = after_enn$x[ncl_focus_neighbors],
      yend = after_enn$y[ncl_focus_neighbors]
    ),
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, color = imb_removed, linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_point(data = ncl_focus_point, size = 4.5, shape = 17, show.legend = FALSE)

n3 <- imb_base(after_enn, "3. Remove the majority neighbors responsible") +
  geom_point(data = after_enn[culprits, ], aes(x, y), inherit.aes = FALSE,
             shape = 4, size = 2.5, stroke = 0.8, color = imb_removed)

n4 <- imb_base(after_enn[-culprits, ], "4. Both passes together")

(n1 + n2) / (n3 + n4) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Like all the methods in this section, this changes the distribution of the training data set, which is covered in @sec-imbalanced-distribution.

## R Examples

```{r}
#| label: ames
#| echo: false
#| message: false
set.seed(1234)
```

We will be using the same subset of the `ames` data set as in the [up-sampling](imbalanced-upsample.qmd) chapter.

```{r}
#| label: show-data
#| message: false
library(recipes)
library(themis)
library(modeldata)
library(dplyr)
data("ames")

ames_imbalance <- ames |>
  filter(MS_Zoning %in% c("Residential_Low_Density", "Residential_Medium_Density")) |>
  mutate(MS_Zoning = droplevels(MS_Zoning)) |>
  select(MS_Zoning, Lot_Area, Year_Built, Gr_Liv_Area, Full_Bath)

ames_imbalance |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```

{themis} provides `step_enn()`.
All three of the variants described above are reachable from this one step.

The `times` argument gives **Repeated Edited Nearest Neighbors**.

```{r}
#| label: step_enn-times
recipe(MS_Zoning ~ ., data = ames_imbalance) |>
  step_enn(MS_Zoning, times = 3) |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL) |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```

And `all_k` gives **AllKNN**.

```{r}
#| label: step_enn-all_k
recipe(MS_Zoning ~ ., data = ames_imbalance) |>
  step_enn(MS_Zoning, all_k = TRUE) |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL) |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```

The **Neighborhood Cleaning Rule** is a separate step, `step_ncl()`.

```{r}
#| label: step_ncl
recipe(MS_Zoning ~ ., data = ames_imbalance) |>
  step_ncl(MS_Zoning) |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL) |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```
